newsitem.title: UK: Politics priced into UK shares, but tremors likely.
newsitem.headline: Politics priced into UK shares, but tremors likely.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party's crushing victory in a key by-election just weeks before Britain goes to the polls was shrugged off by share analysts on Friday who said a Labour general election win was already priced into UK stocks.

But political concerns could still send tremors through the stock market in the run-up to the election as speculation intensifies about the size of Labour's likely majority and the policies it will pursue if it takes office, analysts said.

"The Wirral South result was entirely consistent with national opinion polls," said Robin Aspinall, economist at National Australia Bank. "Like it or not, we will almost certainly have a new government in May."

Although a Labour by-election win was expected at Wirral South, the size of their majority and the turnout were higher than most forecasts. The swing to Labour from the ruling Conservatives was 17.2 percent and the turnout was 73 percent.
"By-election results can be misleading, but not often when they come so close to a general election, with such a big turnout and such a big swing," Aspinall said.

The result led bookmakers William Hill to cut the odds on Labour winning the general election to 2-9 from 1-4. An election must be held by May 22 and May 1 is widely tipped as the most likely date to be chosen by Prime Minister John Major.
But whatever the date, analysts said the by-election confirmed that Major's days were almost certainly numbered.

"It was a complete and utter disaster for John Major. He was slaughtered," one head of equity sales said. "Anyone thinking the Conservatives will make a surge from the back and get into power had better think again."

Markets have traditionally regarded the prospect of a Labour government as a bearish influence. But although the FTSE 100 share index fell on Friday morning, dealers said a weak Dow was behind the move and the by-election result had little impact.
"I don't think it was much of a surprise," said Steve Wright, strategist at BZW. "Most people would suggest that politics is discounted in the market."

Wright said UK shares had lagged the U.S. and Europe in recent months, partly because of the prospect of a Labour government. He said politically sensitive shares, like utilities which may face a "windfall tax" if Labour comes to power, had already priced in a Labour win and were attractively valued.
But although a Labour government was widely regarded as a foregone conclusion, analysts said there was still scope for politics to shake up the stock market as an election approaches.

"As you get closer to the election you're going to see some wobbling and nervousness," Wright said. "People are not quite sure about policy, what Labour are going to do with regard to the corporate sector."
Politics is unlikely to be the dominating influence in the market, however. Wright said company results, international influences and currency factors would all be exerting a pull.
"Politics will just be an extra factor to unsettle the market," he said.

Analysts said Labour's attempts to construct a more credible economic policy had lessened the market's antipathy to a Labour government. Some believe Labour's policies may be preferable to the Conservatives'. But Aspinall at NAB urged caution.

"Even if that view is right, it ignores the fact that it will be a new government, with no experience, a learning curve to go down and mistakes to make," he said. "There will be more post-election uncertainty and disruption than the markets have discounted."
